nameStory: The 'round sardinella' gets its name from its plump, rounded body shape that distinguishes it from other more streamlined sardine-like fish. The name 'sardinella' means 'little sardine' in Latin, reflecting both its small size and its close relationship to the true sardines that have been prized by Mediterranean fishermen for centuries.
description: The round sardinella is a small, silvery fish that looks like a chubby sardine with a distinctly rounded belly. This tropical visitor occasionally shows up in New England's warmer waters, especially during summer months. They're schooling fish that prefer the open ocean, traveling in large groups through warm currents. Most individuals you might encounter are around 6-8 inches long with a compressed, deep body that feels firm and muscular to the touch.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, compressed body with a distinctly rounded belly that feels firm when handled, much more plump than typical herrings

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright silver sides with a blue-green back that has an almost metallic sheen, scales feel smooth and come off easily on your fingers

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single dorsal fin positioned roughly in the middle of the back, with a forked tail fin that feels stiff and strong

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth that opens at the front tip of the snout, designed for filtering small prey from the water

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 6-8 inches long, noticeably smaller than most other schooling fish you'll find in New England waters

habitat: Round sardinellas are warm-water fish that only occasionally visit New England, usually found in offshore waters during the warmest summer months. They prefer the open ocean environment where warm currents bring tropical conditions northward. When present, they're most likely to be encountered by deep-sea fishermen or found washed up on beaches after storms.

seasonality.spring: Rarely present in New England waters as ocean temperatures are still too cool for these tropical fish.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to encounter round sardinellas as warm Gulf Stream waters bring them northward, though sightings remain uncommon.
seasonality.fall: Occasional sightings possible in early fall if warm water conditions persist, but they typically move south as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having returned to their preferred warm southern habitats.

funFact: Round sardinellas are like tiny ocean nomads that follow warm water currents around the world - the same school of fish could travel from the Caribbean to Europe, riding the Gulf Stream like an aquatic highway across the entire Atlantic Ocean!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young herrings or small mackerel, but the round sardinella's distinctly plump, rounded belly and smaller size help distinguish it. Remember: 'round and rare' - if it looks like a chubby sardine in New England waters, it's probably this uncommon visitor.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sardinella,' these fish aren't true sardines, though they're closely related. The name can be confusing since many canned 'sardines' are actually various small fish species, and this tropical visitor represents just one branch of a complex family tree of sardine-like fish.
compareHints: Since round sardinellas are the only members of their genus in our waters, compare them to other small, schooling fish in the herring family. Unlike Atlantic herring, round sardinellas have that characteristic deep, rounded body and prefer much warmer water. They're also smaller and more silvery than the thread herrings and gizzard shads in their family, which tend to be larger with more elongated bodies.
